prompt: What does a delimiter around the customer's message do?
hint: The model sees one stream of text.

choices.text: It hides the message from the model so that it cannot be obeyed
choices.why: The model still reads it; it just knows where it is.

choices.text: It writes down where the customer's words start and end
choices.why: Right, instead of leaving the boundary to a guess.

choices.text: It makes the prompt shorter
choices.why: It adds a few tokens.

choices.text: It turns the message into JSON before the call so the model can parse it
choices.why: The message goes in as text.

prompt: Under `v4-only-json.txt`, the summary for `p01` was the error message the customer pasted. Why, in the stand-in?
hint: What does the stand-in look for before `Message:`?

choices.text: The error message was the longest sentence in the message, so it was picked as the summary
choices.why: Length has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: The prompt had no delimiter, so it took the customer's backticks for one
choices.why: Right: they were the only delimiter in sight.

choices.text: The message was cut at `max_tokens`
choices.why: The reply stopped with `end`.

choices.text: Errors are always sorted as other
choices.why: No such rule; it read the wrong span.

prompt: A prompt ends with `Message: {{message}}` and no delimiter. When does that work?
hint: Two conditions.

choices.text: Whenever the model is large enough to work out the boundary for itself
choices.why: A bigger model still has to guess the boundary.

choices.text: Only when the message is in English
choices.why: Language is not the condition.

choices.text: While it is last and holds nothing like structure
choices.why: Right, and pasted text breaks the second condition.

choices.text: When the temperature is 0
choices.why: Temperature does not move a boundary.

prompt: Why does the section show `v5-backticks.txt` with `cat -n` instead of `cat`?
hint: This page is Markdown.

choices.text: To make the prompt easier to count in tokens, line by line
choices.why: Line numbers have nothing to do with tokens.

choices.text: `cat` refuses files that contain backticks
choices.why: `cat` prints anything.

choices.text: The model reads the line numbers and uses them to find the message
choices.why: The numbers are for the page, not the model.

choices.text: Three backticks would close the page's code block
choices.why: Right: the same failure, one level up.

prompt: Under `v5-backticks.txt`, how many of the six pasted messages passed every check?
hint: The `all` line.

prompt: Under `v5-backticks.txt`, the summary for `p04` was only *When will they try again?* Why?
hint: Count the sets of backticks in the rendered prompt.

choices.text: The stand-in summarises only questions
choices.why: It summarised the courier's note under `v5-tagged`.

choices.text: It took the last pair of backticks
choices.why: Right: the customer's own backticks broke the message in two.

choices.text: The note was too long
choices.why: Length did not matter; the boundary did.

choices.text: The courier's note was in another language
choices.why: It was in English.

prompt: `pl render` warned that the message closes its delimiter; `pl run` said nothing. What habit does that suggest?
hint: When would you ever see the warning?

choices.text: Render a few real cases whenever the template changes, and read the warnings
choices.why: Right: the run renders with warnings off.

choices.text: Ignore the warnings, since the run succeeded
choices.why: It succeeded at producing wrong answers.

choices.text: Delete messages that contain backticks
choices.why: Those are real customers; the template has to cope.

choices.text: Run at a higher temperature to vary the boundary
choices.why: Temperature does not move a boundary.

prompt: A delimiter that the content may contain is a delimiter the content may ___.
hint: What a closing mark does.

prompt: Under `v5-tagged.txt`, how many of the six pasted messages passed every check?
hint: The `all` line.

prompt: From backticks to tags: fixed 4, broken 0, sign test p = 0.125. How should you read that?
hint: Lesson 7: how many changes does the test need?

choices.text: The tags made no difference, since p is above 0.05
choices.why: Above 0.05 means the count cannot show it, not that there is nothing.

choices.text: Too few changes for the test; the replies show the mechanism
choices.why: Right: you can read what each prompt took as the message.

choices.text: p = 0.125 proves the tags are better
choices.why: A p value proves nothing on its own, and this one is not small.

choices.text: Run it again a few times to collect more evidence before deciding
choices.why: At temperature 0 the stand-in gives the same six answers.

prompt: What can a closing tag do that a closing fence of backticks cannot?
hint: `</message>` against three backticks.

choices.text: Name the section it ends
choices.why: Right: a fence closes whatever is open.

choices.text: Stop the model from reading the message
choices.why: The model reads it either way.

choices.text: Escape the text inside it automatically
choices.why: Escaping is a separate step, the `|xml` filter.

choices.text: Make the prompt cheaper than one that uses backticks
choices.why: A tag costs a few more tokens than three backticks.

prompt: Which reasons does the section give for preferring tags? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three reasons, and one claim it rejects.

choices.text: They are rare in what customers write
choices.why: Yes, far rarer than backticks.

choices.text: They have names, so each section can be referred to
choices.why: Yes: the instructions can name `<message>`.

choices.text: Anthropic's documentation recommends them for structuring prompts
choices.why: Yes: *Use XML tags to structure your prompts*.

choices.text: Certain tag names carry a special meaning to models
choices.why: No name is special; consistency is what helps.

prompt: A prompt carries the customer's message, their order record and their last three messages. How do you delimit it?
hint: Each piece of data is a section.

choices.text: One pair of tags around all three
choices.why: Then nothing says where one ends and the next starts.

choices.text: Backticks for the order, tags for the rest
choices.why: Mixing marks gives the content more ways to close one.

choices.text: A named tag for each, referred to by name in the instructions
choices.why: Right, and each value escaped as it goes in.

choices.text: No delimiters, with the instructions placed last
choices.why: Then every boundary is a guess.

prompt: Under `v5-tagged.txt`, `a08` came back with urgency `high`. Why?
hint: Read the rendered prompt as a parser would.

choices.text: The customer was genuinely angry
choices.why: The person who labelled it said normal.

choices.text: Tags make every message more urgent
choices.why: The other pasted messages kept their urgency.

choices.text: The stand-in obeys every message that mentions urgency
choices.why: It obeyed because the line had left the message.

choices.text: Its tag moved a line out
choices.why: Right: its closing tag put the next line among the instructions, and text outside the delimiters is read as one.

prompt: What does `{{message|xml}}` do that `{{message}}` does not?
hint: Compare the two renders of `a08`.

choices.text: Wraps the message in tags
choices.why: The tags are in the template either way.

choices.text: Turns the message into XML elements
choices.why: It does the opposite: tags become plain text.

choices.text: Escapes `<`, `>` and `&` before the value goes in
choices.why: Right, so the customer's text cannot close a tag.

choices.text: Removes anything in the message that looks like an instruction
choices.why: The instruction is still there, inside the message.

prompt: Why could no rewording of the instructions have fixed `a08` under `v5-tagged.txt`?
hint: Who put the line outside the tags?

choices.text: The stand-in ignores instructions
choices.why: It follows them; the trouble is which text counts as one.

choices.text: The template inserted the customer's tag, and with it the boundary
choices.why: Right: the fix belongs in the template, by escaping.

choices.text: Instructions are read after the message
choices.why: Order is not the issue here.

choices.text: A08 is unfixable by design and the case exists to show that some attacks cannot be stopped
choices.why: Escaping fixed it.

prompt: The `v6-escaped` summary for `a08` carries `</message>`. What should a web page that shows it do?
hint: Two formats, two jobs.

choices.text: Turn it back into a real tag before storing it
choices.why: That rebuilds the problem in the next place it is used.

choices.text: Strip everything that looks like a tag
choices.why: That changes what the customer wrote.

choices.text: Nothing; escaped text is safe everywhere
choices.why: It was escaped for the prompt, not for the page.

choices.text: Escape it for HTML, as a separate job
choices.why: Right: each format escapes for itself.

prompt: Put in order the places where the stand-in looks for the message.
hint: Its opening comment lists them.
items: Inside the last pair of triple backticks

prompt: Match each prompt to what happened to it in this lesson.
hint: One each.

pairs.right: The customer's backticks were taken as the delimiter
Four sets of backticks, and the last pair won
A customer's closing tag ended the message early
The whole message stayed inside the tags

prompt: You add a second section to the prompt, `<order>{{order}}</order>`, filled from the order database. What else does it need?
hint: Where does the value come from, and what can it contain?

choices.text: Nothing: database values are trusted
choices.why: A product title or an address in the database was typed by somebody too.

choices.text: Backticks instead of tags, so the two sections differ
choices.why: That brings back the backtick failure.

choices.text: The `|xml` filter: values from outside the template hold whatever was typed into them
choices.why: Right, and a rendered case with a tag in it, to check.

choices.text: A note in the instructions saying the order is safe
choices.why: Wording cannot stop a tag from closing.
